interviewQuestions.question: What's the practical difference between segmentation and paging?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
The shallow answer is "segmentation uses variable-size units, paging uses fixed-size units," which is true but skips the part that matters in an interview: they're solving different problems. Segmentation gives the *programmer's* view of memory — code, stack, heap — a first-class hardware representation, so protection (read-only code, non-executable stack) and sharing (one physical copy of a library's code across processes) fall out naturally, one segment table entry at a time.

Paging has no idea what's inside a page — its entire job is letting a process's memory live in scattered, non-contiguous physical frames without external fragmentation. It's a physical-placement mechanism, not an organizational one.

Because they answer different questions, real systems didn't have to pick one — segmentation-with-paging exists specifically to page each segment internally, keeping the logical boundary while gaining physical flexibility. Modern 64-bit OSes mostly skip the segment table itself and instead get segmentation's protection benefit back via per-page permission bits (read/write/execute, NX) — the idea survived even where the mechanism didn't.

**Testing:** whether you see segmentation and paging as solving different problems rather than as two competing implementations of the same one.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Segmentation vs paging, precisely

interviewQuestions.question: How does segmentation make shared libraries efficient, and does paging lose that benefit?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Under pure segmentation, sharing a library across processes is a one-entry operation: each process's segment table has a code-segment entry pointing at the same physical base address, while its data and stack segments stay private. One physical copy of the library's instructions in RAM serves every process linking it — a real memory savings when dozens of processes share `libc` or a common framework.

Paging doesn't lose this at all — it just implements it at finer granularity. Instead of one segment table entry, the OS maps the same set of physical page frames into multiple processes' page tables, each marked read-only. This is exactly how shared libraries (`.so` files on Linux, DLLs on Windows) actually work today: `mmap` with `MAP_SHARED` or the loader's equivalent, one physical copy, many virtual mappings.

The nuance I'd add: page-level sharing is strictly more flexible than segment-level sharing, because you can share an arbitrary set of pages (say, just the hot code pages) rather than being forced to share or not-share an entire logical segment as a unit.

**Testing:** whether you understand that paging generalized segmentation's sharing trick rather than dropping it.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Shared library memory sharing

interviewQuestions.question: If pure segmentation reintroduces external fragmentation, why was it used at all, and why do modern OSes avoid it?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Segmentation was attractive because it matched how compilers and programmers already structure a program — code, data, stack, heap as separate logical units — and that structure bought protection and sharing almost for free at the hardware level: mark a segment read-only, or point two processes' segment table entries at the same physical memory, and you're done.

The cost is that segments are variable-size by definition, which means placing them in physical memory is the exact bin-packing problem contiguous allocation had — a heap segment that needs to grow might have no free space immediately after it, and general external fragmentation creeps back in as segments of different processes come and go.

Modern OSes sidestep this by paging each segment internally (or, on 64-bit x86, mostly dropping the segment table and using flat paging with per-page protection bits instead) — keeping the logical-protection benefit while eliminating the physical-placement cost. Pure segmentation survives mostly as a history lesson, not a design most systems use today.

**Testing:** whether you can explain segmentation's actual trade-off, not just that it "has fragmentation too."
